topic: straw checkerboard grids that stopped a desert from burying a Chinese railway
title: China Stopped a Desert From Swallowing a Railway — With Dead Grass
description: China's Shapotou Desert Research Station came up with this straw-grid technique in 1955 specifically to stop the Tengger Desert from burying a brand-new railway. Decades later, that same low-tech method has pushed the desert back roughly 25 kilometers along the line it was built to protect.

sources.note: Chinese Academy of Sciences: straw checkerboard grids at Shapotou protect the Baotou-Lanzhou railway from the Tengger Desert.
Overview of the straw checkerboard technique used to stabilize sand dunes and reduce wind erosion.

hook_candidates.text: Stopping a desert from swallowing a railway doesn't need solid barriers — it takes dead grass stuck in a grid.
China stopped a desert from burying a railway using nothing but dead straw pushed into the sand.
How do you stop a sand dune from burying train tracks — using nothing but dead grass?
Two things stopped a desert from burying a railway: dead straw, and a checkerboard pattern.

payoff_mechanism: Each buried straw square breaks up wind at ground level, so blowing sand drops and gets trapped inside the grid instead of piling into dunes, which lets a thin crust and roots form to hold the sand permanently in place.
share_trigger: Send this to the friend who thinks fighting climate problems always needs expensive high-tech solutions, captioned: it's literally dead grass.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume stopping a shifting desert from burying something requires solid barriers like concrete or fences, not dead plant matter.

beats.text: Stopping a desert from swallowing a railway doesn't need solid barriers — it takes **dead grass** stuck in a grid.
In China's Tengger Desert, drifting sand dunes **threatened** a brand-new railway.
Engineers pushed **straw squares** halfway into the sand in a checkerboard.
Each square breaks the wind at ground level — sand drops out of the air and gets **trapped** instead of piling into a dune.
Trapped sand lets roots take hold — the same **dead grass** now anchors a desert that once buried railways. Follow for more.
